Cognitive trajectories
in the perioperative
period.

Anaesthesia, brain topology and brain phenotypes.

Scroll to explore

What is
consciousness?

Not simply a possession, but a process: patterns of activity and relationships that the brain continually enacts.

From this perspective, anaesthesia changes how those relationships operate. The transitions themselves become the object of study.

The same room.
Different worlds of experience.

Brightness, colour, perception — reconfigured.

An apparently still body cannot tell us the content of an inner world.

Two brains can appear equally unresponsive.
What happens within need not be identical.

The outside does not reveal
the inside.

Two patients may be equally unresponsive to a command, yet this observation alone cannot tell us whether experience is absent, altered, inaccessible, or simply not remembered.

Behavioural responsiveness, conscious experience and later recollection are related, but distinct questions.

Responsiveness

What can we observe?

Movement, command-following and reaction to stimulation are observable behaviours. Their absence does not by itself specify all neural or subjective states.

Experience

What may be happening?

Drug-specific alterations of large-scale dynamics may change how sensory information, memory, self and time are related.

Recollection

What can be reported?

Amnesia after emergence tells us about memory formation or access. It is not logically identical to proof that nothing was experienced.

Phenomenology begins where behaviour is insufficient.

We can infer, measure and model brain dynamics. But any claim about an individual's subjective experience needs more caution than a clean curve or a single monitor value permits.

Different drugs.
Different transitions.

The original illustrations describe different phenomenological possibilities — not anaesthetic concentrations, EEG signatures or a clock measuring subjective time.

The four drawn forms below are deliberately redrawn to match the original presentation: a closed loop, a jagged detour, a sleep-like dip and irregular oscillations.

Propofol

Induction → an unremembered interval → emergence

Ketamine

Potential dissociation and alteration of experienced sequence

Dexmedetomidine

Sleep-like sedation, sometimes readily reversible with stimulation

Sevoflurane

These shapes reproduce the original visual analogy. Their vertical fluctuations are not quantitative indices of consciousness or elapsed time; different patients may report different experiences or no recall.

A schematic exploration of phenomenology, not a claim that a particular anaesthetic guarantees unconsciousness, absence of experience, dreaming or specific memories.

The brain is
a dynamic system.

Even at rest, its networks continuously reorganise. Activity is not static: the brain moves among many possible configurations.

A moving flock provides an intuition: coherent patterns emerge without each element remaining in the same position.

Fractals.
Patterns at different scales.

Complex systems can produce structure from simple local rules. Branching, repetition, and changes in scale give us a language for patterns that are neither random nor rigid.

A fractal is a mathematical structure with scale-dependent or self-similar detail. A flock or a road network is an analogy for self-organisation — not necessarily a mathematically exact fractal.

Complexity from recurrence

One branching rule, repeated across scales, can generate a rich structure. The brain's network organisation also operates across nested spatial and temporal scales, though it is not a literal copy of this mathematical tree.

8 levels

How is the brain
connected?

Three different questions about the same network.

Structural connectivity

The physical wiring: axons and white-matter pathways connecting brain regions.

Anatomical pathways

Small changes.
Sudden transitions.

In a nonlinear system, gradually varying an input can produce an abrupt reorganisation of its behaviour.

Bifurcations, fluid phase diagrams and collective movement offer ways of thinking about these changes. They are analogies—not literal mathematical descriptions of anaesthetic consciousness.

From one stable pattern to many

Stable behaviourIncreasingly complex behaviour

A classic nonlinear-systems model of bifurcation, not a patient measurement.

Metastability
and attractors.

A flexible brain can revisit multiple relatively stable network configurations. An attractor is a state toward which a system tends to settle.

Anaesthetic drugs reshape the landscape of available states. One way to visualise this is movement among shallow valleys giving way to fewer, deeper ones.

Multiple nearby valleys illustrate a greater repertoire of possible transitions.

An illustrative state-space landscape. Its valleys are a metaphor for dynamical tendencies, not a direct scan of the brain.

Explore the full metastability illustration

An expanded view of network states and attractor landscapes.

The brain phenotype defines
stability — or fragility.

A brain does not arrive in theatre as a blank slate. Its synapses, connectivity, chemistry, immune state, prior experiences and capacity to adapt form a particular starting configuration.

The original four-factor illustration can be rebuilt as a living model. None of its components alone determines an outcome, and chronological age is not equivalent to brain fragility.

✳

Synaptic density

The quantity and organisation of local connections. Not simply “more is better”: pruning and refinement also support efficient function.

Local processing and plasticity
⌘

Connectivity

White-matter architecture, network integration, alternate routes, and coordination across distributed regions.

Integration and redundancy
⇄

Neurochemistry

Cholinergic, monoaminergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic and other signalling systems shape network responsiveness.

Excitation, inhibition and modulation
✺

Inflammation

Immune activation, underlying disease and the inflammatory response to surgery can modify brain function.

The physiological environment

Two contrasting network architectures

Illustrative phenotypes — not a diagnostic scan of a young person versus an older person.

More flexible / higher reserve

Greater route redundancy, integration and capacity to reorganise despite a disturbance.

same
perturbation⟶

More vulnerable / lower reserve

Less redundancy or fewer compensatory pathways may leave less room to absorb stress.

Both networks are visible. Explore how the same challenge can have different effects on their organisation.

Same anaesthetic. Different brain. Potentially different recovery.

The comparison illustrates susceptibility, not fate. Frailty, dementia, prior stroke, sensory impairment, sleep, physiology, medicines, operative stress, and the quality of perioperative care can modify the outcome. Older people vary enormously.

Phenotype is more than anatomy

It includes both relatively enduring characteristics and fluctuating state: sleep, acute illness, pain, medications, stress, inflammation and sensory input. A brain's “reserve” is not a single measurable tank; it is a useful way to discuss resilience across systems.

A changing response surface

We often observe the clinical expression — attention, wakefulness, memory, independence — rather than the entire underlying network state. Interpreting those outcomes requires an individual baseline.

A phenotype is
a lifelong trajectory.

The brain we meet in the operating theatre is the current expression of a developmental history, biological adaptation, learning, illness and recovery.

Age alters probabilities, not certainties. An active older adult and a younger patient with multimorbidity can have quite different forms of vulnerability.

Early life — rapid development

Connectivity is being formed and reshaped. This visual is illustrative and does not depict a validated age-specific brain biomarker.

Select any point on the timeline to bring its network illustration into focus; all stages remain visible above.

A trace of
changing states.

Processed EEG and spectral displays offer glimpses of how population-level brain activity shifts during anaesthesia.

Anaesthetic monitoring provides examples of these changes. They provide visual context for these transitions without being simple, one-to-one measures of subjective experience.

Delirium is not just confusion.

It is an acute, usually fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, commonly accompanied by changes in cognition, perception, sleep-wake rhythm and activity. A quiet, withdrawn patient can have delirium as surely as an agitated one.

The network illustration, rebuilt

From the original five-stage concept: a vulnerable system is perturbed, coordination may fragment, and reorganisation may be impaired.

BaselineIntegrated and adaptable

Coordinated network activity with alternative pathways.

PerturbationPhysiological stress

Pain, inflammation, drugs, infection, sleep and metabolic insults.

DisorganisationReduced integration

Connectivity and coordination may become disrupted.

Reintegration difficultyTransitions remain unstable

A hypothesised difficulty finding a stable, coherent configuration.

Clinical deliriumAcute and fluctuating

Attention, awareness and cognition change over hours or days.

An important distinction

“Failure to reintegrate” is an explanatory hypothesis and visual metaphor, not an established diagnostic definition or single proven mechanism. Delirium is multifactorial and frequently treatable; infection, hypoxia, drug effects, pain, dehydration and other causes require clinical assessment.

What changes clinically?

◌

Attention

Difficulty concentrating, tracking conversation or shifting focus.

◐

Awareness

Altered arousal and orientation; activity and responsiveness fluctuate.

≈

Perception & thought

Misinterpretations, hallucinations, disorganised thinking or new fear.

⌁

Sleep & behaviour

Reversed sleep rhythm, withdrawal, agitation or changing psychomotor activity.

Hyperactive

Restless, distressed, agitated, sometimes hypervigilant.

Hypoactive

Quiet, slowed, drowsy, withdrawn — easily mistaken for tiredness or normal recovery.

Mixed

Alternating between apparently opposing states during the same illness.

Attractor landscapes, revisited.

The original valley analogy can illustrate reduced flexibility or unstable transitions. Delirium does not necessarily mean that no stable attractor exists, and these diagrams cannot diagnose it.

Many accessible configurations

Perturbed landscape

Narrowed repertoire

Delirium and persistent cognitive change are related questions — not synonyms.

Delirium is temporally defined by acute onset and fluctuation. Longer-term cognitive trajectories require an understanding of the person's preoperative cognition and subsequent recovery. Associations between delirium and later decline do not, alone, establish a unique causal pathway.

For clinical assessment, NICE recommends the 4AT when indicators are identified, and CAM-ICU or ICDSC in recovery or critical care. NICE CG103 recommendations. Terminology: 2018 perioperative neurocognitive nomenclature recommendations.

These questions
are not new.

Concerns about mental and cognitive change after anaesthesia predate modern brain-network science.

1887

George Henry Savage

“Insanity following the Use of Anaesthetics in Operations” was an early attempt to describe mental disturbance after operations.

1955

P. D. Bedford

“Adverse Cerebral Effects of Anaesthesia on Old People” helped frame the enduring concern about cognition after anaesthesia in older patients.

Different eras used different language and methods. The central question persists: what changes after surgery, and what was already changing beforehand?

Historical labels such as “insanity” and “POCD” are retained only to identify the original works, not as present-day diagnoses.

A single score is
not a trajectory.

Cognition may be changing before an operation; afterwards, patients may recover, follow an existing trend, or experience different degrees of lasting change.

The crucial question is what happened before, around and after surgery—rather than treating one postoperative measurement as a complete explanation.

At the operation

All four trajectories remain visible throughout. Select a label to bring one into focus; scrub across time to see how their relative positions change. These are schematic, not observed patient data or proof of causality.

Phenotype also
changes over a lifetime.

Synaptic networks change across life: connections proliferate and are selectively refined as the brain develops.

Development and ageing represent different starting architectures. They raise different questions about the effects of perturbation, recovery and longer-term outcomes.

The developmental illustration is a conceptual explanation of synaptic formation and pruning; it does not by itself establish long-term anaesthetic neurotoxicity in humans.

From networks to evidence

What can the latest research
actually tell us?

A series of visual investigations — beginning with how to interpret a brain scan, then moving through consciousness, individuality, the life course and postoperative delirium.

When two regions move together,
does one cause the other?

Functional connectivity usually describes correlations between fluctuating signals. Correlated signals do not necessarily mean that two regions communicate directly — or that one causes the other to change.

A brain scan offers a window into organised activity, not an unmediated picture of thought or proof of its cause.

Context for the illustrationsJang et al. · Nature Communications · 2024Fotiadis et al. · Communications Biology · 2025
Consciousness · network organisation

The brain needs separation
and connection.

Specialised communities must retain their identity while exchanging information with other communities. Under propofol, fMRI studies observe a shift in this balance.

Conscious brain organisation may depend less on the number of connections than on the balance between local processing and global exchange.

SourcesJang et al. · Nat Commun 15, 9164 (2024)Luppi et al. · Nat Commun 15, 2171 (2024)
Unresponsiveness ≠ absence of experience

Similar behaviour.
Different internal dynamics.

In the EEG study, propofol, xenon and ketamine all produced unresponsiveness. Yet reports of conscious, dream-like experiences and measures of critical dynamics differed.

Absence of a response is a behavioural finding. Experience and neural dynamics require other evidence.

SourcesMaschke et al. · Commun Biol 7, 946 (2024)Fotiadis et al. · Commun Biol 8, 1254 (2025)
Brain phenotype · functional individuality

Every brain has
a recognisable pattern.

Under general anaesthesia, the functional connectomes in one study became less distinguishable between people. The pattern of individuality was temporarily reduced — then recovered.

The phenotype is not merely anatomy: its functional expression changes with state.

SourceLuppi et al. · Nature Human Behaviour 9, 987–1004 (2025)
Life course · cognitive reserve

The brain arrives at surgery
with a history.

Functional network organisation changes nonlinearly across the lifespan. At any age, two people with similar pathological burdens may demonstrate different cognitive function.

Age is a crude descriptor. Development, disease, adaptation and reserve create different starting points for the same surgical challenge.

SourcesSun et al. · Nature Neuroscience 28, 891–901 (2025)Vockert et al. · Nat Commun 15, 9815 (2024)
Delirium · susceptibility and stress

Why the same operation
is not the same event
for every brain.

Preoperative cognition, inflammation, underlying pathology and acute physiological insults can converge. The studies report associations, not a deterministic formula for who develops delirium.

Delirium is better approached as an interaction between who the patient is and what the patient encounters.

SourcesFeinkohl et al. · Scientific Reports 15 (2025)Hansen et al. · Molecular Psychiatry (published 2025)
Delirium · biology beyond neurons

A disturbed brain network
has a cellular environment.

A small human neurosurgical multi-omics study found delirium-associated differences in glial inflammatory and synaptic pathways. This adds a biological layer to the network diagrams — without proving a single causal mechanism.

Network dysfunction may be the visible consequence of changes in neurons, glia, circulation and inflammation together.

SourcesIshii et al. · Molecular Psychiatry (2026)Boesen et al. · Nature Reviews Neurology 22, 309–323 (2026) · hypothesis
From patterns to patients

A promising model
is not yet a clinical answer.

Intraoperative EEG may contain information associated with postoperative delirium. But a strong discrimination statistic is not the same as a reliable answer for the next individual patient.

A useful biomarker must do more than correlate with an outcome: it must produce accurate, actionable predictions in real-world patients.

SourceAhn et al. · npj Digital Medicine 8, 661 (2025)

Anaesthesia is the art of guiding a complex brain through unstable transitions while respecting the unique phenotype of that brain.
